Inhabitant
in-HAB-i-tant
n. (rendering Hebrew yōshēb and Greek katoikeō, katoikōn)
From Latin inhabitare, to dwell in — in plus habitare, to have habitually, to dwell. The Hebrew is the active participle of yāshab, to sit or dwell, so that an inhabitant is literally one sitting in a place: the same verb behind sit. Dwelling in Scripture's idiom is a settled sitting rather than a mere location, and the inhabitants of a land are those who have taken their seat in it.

Biblical Definition

Scripture speaks of inhabitants in order to say two things about them: they are small before God, and they are accountable to Him. The smallness is Isaiah's: “It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers; that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain” (Isa 40:22). The comparison is not contempt but proportion, and the chapter uses it to comfort a people who thought their way was hid from the LORD. The accountability is everywhere: “The earth also is defiled under the inhabitants thereof; because they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, broken the everlasting covenant” (Isa 24:5) — a remarkable verse, since it charges the whole earth's population with breach of a covenant, which points back past Sinai to the creation ordinance and the covenant with Noah binding on all mankind. The proper response of inhabitants to their Maker is therefore reverence: “Let all the earth fear the LORD: let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him” (Psa 33:8). And the term carries an eschatological weight in Revelation, where the dwellers on earth are those whose settled home and hope are here: “Woe to the inhabiters of the earth and of the sea! for the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath, because he knoweth that he hath but a short time” (Rev 12:12). Against them stand the saints, who are strangers and pilgrims, inhabitants of no city they can see.

Webster 1828 Definition

One who dwells or resides permanently in a place; in Scripture the earth's population viewed under God — as grasshoppers before His greatness, as accountable for a defiled earth and a broken everlasting covenant, and as summoned to stand in awe of Him.

INHABITANT, n. 1. One who dwells or resides permanently in a place, or who has a fixed residence, as distinguished from an occasional lodger or visitor.

2. In Scripture, the word renders a Hebrew participle signifying one sitting or settled in a place; hence dwelling denotes a settled abode, and not mere presence.

3. The inhabitants of the earth; mankind considered as dwelling upon it under the government of God. Psalm 33; Isa. 24.

4. The inhabiters of the earth; in the Apocalypse, those whose portion and hope are in this world only. Rev. 12.

5. Inhabitant of a land, in the law of the jubile; every man to whom liberty was proclaimed in the fiftieth year. Levit. 25.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 40:22 — "It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers; that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in:"

Isaiah 24:5 — "The earth also is defiled under the inhabitants thereof; because they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, broken the everlasting covenant."

Psalm 33:8 — "Let all the earth fear the LORD: let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him."

Revelation 12:12 — "Therefore rejoice, ye heavens, and ye that dwell in them. Woe to the inhabiters of the earth and of the sea! for the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath, because he knoweth that he hath but a short time."

Modern Corruption

Isa 24:5 is the verse most needed and least used in modern discussion of the earth's condition, because it locates the defilement in the moral breach of a covenant by the inhabitants rather than merely in their mismanagement of resources.

expand to see more

Two frameworks now compete for the subject, and Scripture belongs to neither. One treats the earth as raw material with no claim on its inhabitants beyond usefulness, which cannot be squared with a creation God pronounced good, a land given sabbaths of its own, and a law that forbids taking the mother bird with the young. The other treats the earth as itself sacred and man as essentially a contaminant, which cannot be squared with Gen 1:28 or with the fact that man alone bears the image of God. Isa 24 gives the third account and the truer one: the earth is defiled under its inhabitants because they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, and broken the everlasting covenant. The disorder in the ground is downstream of the disorder in the man, exactly as Gen 3 said — cursed is the ground for thy sake.

The pastoral use of the doctrine is in the contrast Revelation draws. The dwellers on the earth are not simply people who happen to live here; the phrase marks those whose settled portion is here and who have no other. Believers are called strangers and pilgrims, whose citizenship is in heaven, and who therefore hold their tenancy loosely without holding it carelessly. That is why the Christian can be the best possible steward of a place he does not ultimately belong to: he tends it as a trust rather than clutching it as a possession, he expects no paradise from it, and he is not driven to despair when it fails him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yōshēb is the participle of yāshab, to sit or dwell — an inhabitant is one sitting in a place. Greek katoikeō is to settle down and dwell, distinguished from paroikeō, to sojourn as a stranger.

expand to see more

Hebrew yōshēb (H3427, participle) — one dwelling, an inhabitant; from yāshab, to sit, remain, dwell.

Hebrew tēbēl (H8398) — the habitable world; the term in Psa 33:8, all the inhabitants of the world, viewing the earth as inhabited rather than as mere ground.

Greek katoikeō (G2730) — to dwell, settle, inhabit; used of them that dwell on the earth throughout Revelation.

Greek paroikeō (G3939) — to sojourn, dwell as a stranger; the contrasting word, from which parish derives, used of Abraham sojourning in the land of promise.

Greek oikoumenē (G3625) — the inhabited world; rendered the world in the decree of Caesar Augustus that all the world should be taxed (Luk 2:1).

Usage

"Of the creature's smallness before God: the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers (Isa 40:22)."

"Of accountability and defilement: the earth is defiled under the inhabitants thereof (Isa 24:5); let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him (Psa 33:8)."

"Of those whose portion is here: woe to the inhabiters of the earth (Rev 12:12), set against the saints who are strangers and pilgrims (Heb 11:13)."
